conventional_description: Heel pain is most commonly caused by plantar fasciitis, an inflammation of the thick band of tissue that runs across the bottom of the foot. The hallmark symptom is a sharp, stabbing pain in the bottom of the heel, especially with the first steps in the morning or after periods of rest. Other causes include heel spurs, Achilles tendinitis, stress fractures, and nerve entrapment. Diagnosis is usually based on a physical exam and symptom history, with imaging reserved for cases that don't respond to initial treatment.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on reducing inflammation and mechanical stress. This includes rest, ice, stretching exercises, supportive footwear, and over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medications. For persistent cases, doctors may recommend custom orthotics, night splints, physical therapy, corticosteroid injections, or shockwave therapy. Surgery is a last resort for those who do not improve after many months of conservative care.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands heel pain primarily through the Kidney and Liver systems. The Kidney channel runs directly through the heel, and the Kidneys govern the bones and store essence. When Kidney Yin or essence is depleted - often with age, overwork, or chronic stress - the heel loses its foundational support, leading to a dull, achy pain that worsens with standing and eases with rest. The Liver, which nourishes the sinews and tendons, also plays a role: Liver Blood deficiency can leave the plantar fascia dry and brittle, prone to micro-tears.
But not all heel pain is due to deficiency. Sometimes the problem is stagnation - blood and Qi get stuck in the local channels, causing a sharp, fixed pain that doesn't let up with rest. This often follows an old injury or years of prolonged standing. Dampness and heat can also settle into the foot, creating a swollen, burning sensation that feels worse with warmth. Each of these mechanisms produces a distinct pain quality, which is why a TCM practitioner will ask not just “where does it hurt?” but “what does it feel like?”
This is the core insight: one Western diagnosis of plantar fasciitis can have multiple TCM root causes. The treatment that works for a construction worker with blood stasis will be very different from the one that helps a middle-aged office worker with Kidney Yin deficiency. By matching the treatment to the pattern, TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalance, not just silence the pain signal.
classical_quote: 「骨者，髓之府，不能久立，行则振掉，骨将惫矣。」
classical_translation: "The bones are the storehouse of the marrow; if one cannot stand for long and sways when walking, the bones are becoming exhausted. This reflects the Kidney's role in nourishing bones and marrow, and why deficiency leads to heel pain on standing."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner starts by asking what the heel pain feels like. A dull, sore ache (隐痛, yǐn tòng) that worsens after long standing or walking and eases with rest points toward Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency. This pattern is common in middle age and beyond. The tongue looks red with little coating, and the pulse feels deep and thready (沉细脉, chén xì mài). Additional clues include achy low back and knees, dizziness, or ringing in the ears.
Sharp, stabbing pain (刺痛, cì tòng) fixed in one spot suggests Qi and Blood Stagnation. The heel hurts more with direct pressure, and there may be a history of an old injury or prolonged standing. Unlike the dull ache of deficiency, this pain does not improve with rest and can even worsen at night. The tongue may appear dark purple with small red or purple spots, and the pulse feels wiry or rough (涩脉, sè mài).
A mild but persistent dull ache accompanied by foot weakness points to Qi and Blood Deficiency. The pain is more of a constant background ache than a sharp signal. The person often looks pale, feels generally tired, and has a pale tongue with a thin white coat. The pulse is thin and weak (细弱脉, xì ruò mài). Because the body lacks the nourishment to repair sinews, the ache lingers even without heavy use.
If the heel feels swollen, hot, or burning, Damp Heat in the Channels is likely. This pattern is less common but quite distinct. The tongue coating appears thick and greasy - yellow if heat dominates, white if dampness is heavier - and the pulse feels slippery and possibly rapid (滑数脉, huá shuò mài). The pain may flare in humid weather or after rich, greasy food. Unlike cold-type pain, warmth offers no relief and can make it worse.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, aching heel pain", "Worse with prolonged standing or walking", "Better with rest", "Soreness and weakness of the lower back and knees", "Dizziness, tinnitus, or dry eyes", "Night sweats, dry mouth, or heat in palms and soles"]
patterns.worse_with: Prolonged standing or walking, Overwork and chronic lack of sleep, Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Stress or emotional frustration, Excessive sexual activity
patterns.better_with: Rest and elevating the foot, Gentle massage of foot and calf, Supportive, cushioned shoes, Adequate sleep and hydration
patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidney channel runs through the heel, and the Kidneys govern the bones while the Liver governs the sinews. When Kidney and Liver Yin are depleted, there is not enough essence and blood to nourish the heel area, so the bones and soft tissues become weak and malnourished. This “malnourishment pain” (不荣则痛) feels like a dull ache that intensifies after prolonged standing or walking, because weight-bearing further strains the undernourished heel, and eases with rest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine and rapid, wiry, weak at the left Chi (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Liver Yin are the deep reserves of the body. Overuse, prolonged weight-bearing, and insufficient rest drain these reserves further, making the undernourished heel hurt more. Rest allows the body to conserve and rebuild Yin. Spicy and drying foods create internal heat that consumes Yin fluids, while moistening, Yin-nourishing foods replenish them. Emotional frustration stirs Liver Yang, which uses up Yin, so a calm mind protects the body’s nourishing resources.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat foods that gently nourish Yin, such as black sesame seeds, walnuts, goji berries, mulberries, pears, and lightly cooked leafy greens. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods, and limit coffee and alcohol, which can deplete Yin fluids. Prioritize adequate rest and avoid standing or walking for long periods without breaks. Supportive shoes with good cushioning can reduce strain on the heel. Gentle evening stretching of the calves and feet helps maintain flexibility without overtaxing the body.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and blood fail to flow smoothly through the channels of the foot, the local tissues become starved of nourishment and choked with waste. This stagnation often follows a past injury, repetitive strain, or years of prolonged standing. The result is a fixed, stabbing pain deep in the heel that feels worse with pressure, as the stuck blood and Qi create a local blockage that the body cannot easily resolve on its own.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry and choppy (弦涩 xián sè), like a taut string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Warmth and gentle movement invigorate Qi and blood, helping to break up the local stagnation that causes the stabbing pain. Cold and prolonged pressure, on the other hand, congeal blood and worsen the blockage, making the pain more intense and fixed.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the feet warm and avoid prolonged standing on hard surfaces. Gentle daily stretching of the calf and plantar fascia, along with warm foot soaks, helps keep blood moving. Limit cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which can congeal blood and worsen stasis.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When Qi and Blood are deficient, the body lacks the resources to nourish the sinews and muscles of the feet. The heel, which bears the body's weight, receives even less nourishment, leading to a persistent dull ache.
Unlike sharp pain from stagnation or burning pain from damp heat, this ache feels weak and achy, like the foot is simply tired and underfed. It often comes with overall fatigue, pale complexion, and dizziness because the whole body is running low on energy and blood.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and weak (弱 ruò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: When Qi and Blood are deficient, the body needs rest and nourishment to rebuild its reserves. Overexertion, poor diet, and stress further deplete these resources, making the dull ache worse. Warmth and gentle movement encourage circulation without draining energy, while nourishing foods directly supply the building blocks for Qi and Blood, easing the weakness and pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like bone broths, congees, dark leafy greens, red dates, and goji berries. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax digestion. Gentle movement like walking or tai chi can help Qi and Blood flow without depleting reserves, but rest when tired.

patterns.why_this_happens: Dampness and Heat are a sticky, inflammatory pair that can settle into the channels of the foot when your body struggles with chronic damp-heat or is exposed to hot, humid environments. Dampness is heavy and sinks downward, obstructing the flow of Qi and blood in the heel, while Heat creates redness, swelling, and a burning sensation. Together they make the area feel hot, swollen, and exquisitely tender, especially when pressed.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-heat thrives on warmth and moisture, so cold packs and dry conditions directly counteract the swelling and burning pain. Spicy and greasy foods add fuel to internal heat and create more dampness, while rest reduces the mechanical irritation that inflames the already obstructed channels.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sugary foods that generate dampness and heat. Choose cooling, damp-draining foods like barley, mung beans, celery, and cucumber. Keep the feet cool and dry; avoid hot soaks or heating pads. Gentle movement is fine, but rest during acute flare-ups to reduce friction.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help heel pain?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture works locally to release tight muscles, improve circulation, and calm inflammation right at the painful spot. Points like Kunlun (BL-60) and Taixi (KI-3) are often used. Many patients feel immediate relief after a session, though lasting change requires a series of treatments to address the root pattern.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: A typical course is 6-10 weekly sessions, though this varies by pattern and chronicity. Acute blood stasis pain may resolve in just a few visits, while long-standing Kidney deficiency may need ongoing treatment for a few months. Your practitioner will reassess progress every 3-4 weeks and adjust the plan accordingly.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with my current treatments?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes. Acupuncture and herbal medicine can complement orthotics, physical therapy, and NSAIDs. However, if you are taking blood thinners, let your TCM practitioner know, as some herbs (like Dang Gui or Chuan Xiong) may have mild blood-moving effects. Always keep both your doctor and TCM practitioner informed of all treatments you are receiving.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Dietary advice is gentle and supportive. In general, favor warm, cooked foods and avoid icy drinks and raw foods, which can weaken digestion and create dampness. If your pattern is Kidney deficiency, bone broths and black-colored foods (black beans, black sesame) are especially nourishing. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Can TCM treat plantar fasciitis permanently?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to resolve the underlying imbalance so that pain does not return. When the root pattern is corrected - whether that means replenishing Kidney Yin or moving stagnant blood - many people experience lasting relief. However, lifestyle factors like prolonged standing or poor footwear can recreate the conditions for pain, so maintenance and self-care are important.

faqs.question: Does TCM work for heel spurs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Heel spurs in TCM are seen as a manifestation of Kidney deficiency (bone overgrowth) or chronic blood stasis. While herbs and acupuncture cannot dissolve the spur, they can reduce the inflammation and soft-tissue pain around it, often making the spur asymptomatic. Many people with spurs find they can walk comfortably again after treatment.

faqs.question: Are there any side effects from the herbs?
faqs.answer: TCM herbal formulas are prescribed specifically for your pattern and are generally well tolerated. Occasional mild digestive upset can occur when starting a new formula, but this usually settles quickly. Your practitioner will select herbs carefully, especially if you have a sensitive stomach or are on other medications. Always report any unexpected reactions.

research.title: The effectiveness of acupuncture for plantar heel pain: a systematic review
research.description: This systematic review evaluated RCTs of acupuncture for plantar heel pain. It found moderate evidence that acupuncture reduces pain and improves function compared to standard care or sham, with effects lasting up to 4 weeks. The review highlighted the need for larger, high-quality trials.
research.periodical: Clark RJ, Tighe M. The effectiveness of acupuncture for plantar heel pain: a systematic review. Acupunct Med. 2012;30(4):298-306.

research.title: Effectiveness of acupuncture for plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This RCT compared acupuncture to sham acupuncture and standard care in 80 patients. The acupuncture group showed significantly greater improvements in pain and foot function at 4 and 8 weeks, supporting acupuncture as an effective treatment for plantar fasciitis.
research.periodical: Kumnerddee W, Pattapong N. Effectiveness of acupuncture for plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial. Med Acupunct. 2012;24(4):233-238.

research.title: Clinical observation on Duhuo Jisheng Decoction combined with acupuncture for plantar fasciitis
research.description: In this study, 60 patients with plantar fasciitis of Kidney deficiency and cold-damp pattern were treated with modified Duhuo Jisheng Decoction plus acupuncture. After 4 weeks, 85% reported significant pain reduction, suggesting that combined herbal and acupuncture therapy addresses both root and branch.
research.periodical: Zhang X, Li Y, Wang H. Clinical observation on Duhuo Jisheng Decoction combined with acupuncture for plantar fasciitis. Chin J Inf Tradit Chin Med. 2017;24(3):68-70.
